#896. How to make failure your friend and teacher in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

How can the apprenticeship model and its focus on practice making perfect apply to science?Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Roger Kneebone’s 2020 book Expert compares molecular scientists to Savile Row tailors, lacemakers to vascular surgeons. Kneebone, a former trauma surgeon who how leads a master’s programme in surgical education at Imperial College London, says the road to professional expertise begins with an “apprentice” phase, doing monotonous tasks repeatedly and learning from mistakes.

Ruth Morgan, a crime and forensic science researcher at University College London, says: “Whether you’re learning to do a titration in the lab, or whether you’re learning to cut material as a tailor, there are so many mistakes that you make in that process. And that’s kind of the point. Every time you make a mistake you get better, and there’s a huge amount of time spent doing that.”

Earlier this year, Morgan joined Kneebone at a conference session on failure and expertise, part of a one-day failure in science conference, held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

In the fourth episode of a six-part podcast series that revisits some of the conference themes, Morgan says successful collaborations across scientific disciplines rely on individual researchers seeing themselves as “outsiders, beginners”, unafraid of asking questions. “That’s incredibly scary” she says, “because it means you have to concede that you don’t know something, and you’re having to ask.

“It’s quite a distinctive skillset to cultivate. You have to be willing to be uncomfortable, to really drill into what you know, but what you don’t know, and to become a really good listener, so that you can hear what somebody else in a different space sees or knows."

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03654-3

We talked about the taxonomy of failure and how that can look throughout the life cycle of expertise, as a necessary companion, and a teacher, that is on the journey with us as we go from being essentially an apprentice through to becoming more expert.

That’s Professor Ruth Morgan reporting back from the failure and expertise session in a conference held at Imperial College London, in April 2026.

We talked about intrinsic failure that seems to be inherent whenever you’re working at intersections, whether that’s an intersection of two different disciplines that maybe look at failure or perceive failure in different ways.

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

In episode four of this series about failure in science, we explore the benefits and the pitfalls of being an expert in your field.

The thread that really brought all that together was this idea of the potential for failure and the pain.

So, the importance of the wrestle, which is a term I’ve been thinking about a lot recently.

We have to create spaces to be able to wrestle with an idea, with the potential for failure, with difference of perspectives, difference of opinion, different ways of seeing things.

The pain is there in both in the way they come together is quite deeply and profoundly part of being human, and part of innovation and discovery and curiosity.

So I’m Professor Ruth Morgan. I’m based at UCL and professor of crime and forensic science.

Anyone who’s been working in this kind of space for any length of time can think of far too many personal failures.

But I guess a very public one that I can share with you was when I set about trying to crowdfund a very large sum of money to build an evidence interpretation lab, which would have been the first one in the world.

And I actually even ended up working with a big advertising agency, and we had we had billboards on buses through London.

We had a film that was in every single independent cinema in the UK for four months, I think.

And it was incredible. It was a beautiful piece of storytelling, and we raised about £4.25. The target was a million, so we fell short there. So that was a fairly public failure.

So in the failure and expertise session that we had at the conference, our discussion was curated and led by Professor Roger Kneebone, who’s the author of the book Expert, and he talks very beautifully about this journey that you go on from being an apprentice, building your expertise to the point where you become an expert.

And one of the things that we really explored in that conversation was around how, when you’re learning as an apprentice, you have to do the same task again and again and again.

It’s very monotonous. And there’s a huge amount of failure involved in that.

So, whether you’re learning to do a titration in the lab, or whether you’re learning to cut material as a tailor, there are so many mistakes that you make in that process.

Every time you make a mistake you get better, and there’s a huge amount of time spent doing that.

And it’s only as you go through that do you start finding the little shortcuts and heuristics and ways of seeing it that you have gained through all of those failures, and to the point of then becoming able to then teach others and be seen as an expert.

So there’s this idea that failure becomes something of a companion as you go through that journey. And it’s absolutely intrinsic to building expertise, to gaining that craft.

So the Heurista Institute came about, we got to this idea that there are an awful lot of complex challenges in the world, and you could argue that in many ways they’re getting more complex.

So the more you can explore them, the more you know about them, actually, the more complex they get.

What if the answer to a lot of these problems is less about creating new knowledge, and it’s more about bringing together existing forms of knowledge, but in different ways, asking different questions, and making connections that maybe haven’t been made before that move us forward in a sort of stepwise change moment?

So it’s about how do we bring those different perspectives together, those different disciplines together, in a structure within a university which is quite delineated by disciplines, and those boundaries are often quite clear.

And also, how do we traverse and bridge the boundaries that exist with and around that university system, with industry, with government, with other sectors where that insight is needed, and who can actually do stuff with it and actually make a difference?

And so we, yeah, so that’s how the institute came about.

Can we bridge those gaps between disciplines, and can we bridge the boundaries that exist between the university and the real world?

One of the things that is extraordinary about working at these intersections between different disciplines is that it really opens up the opportunity to be an outsider, to be a beginner, and to ask questions.

And that’s incredibly scary, because it means you have to concede that you don’t know, you don’t know something, and you’re having to ask.

But it also levels the field, if you like, and it actually makes people more open to asking those questions and being challenged in ways that help you see things in different ways that you might not have been able to see in a different context.

So it’s quite a distinctive skillset to cultivate.

You have to be willing to be uncomfortable, to really drill into what you know, but what you don’t know, and to become a really good listener, so that you can hear what somebody else in a different space sees or knows.

And then start that translation work, of translating between those different perspectives.

One of the things that we’ve really noticed in the work that we do is that our sort of starting point was we want to bring all these different perspectives together so that we can find the points of resonance, the places where people agree, because that will really help us at these intersections, work out maybe where to go next.

So failure in that sense, I think, is very, very interesting because, in some ways, you’re having to unlearn everything you’ve learnt What it means to be an expert in a particular discipline, you have to be willing to put that down in some ways, and to come into a space that you don’t understand.

And what does it mean for trust in science? I think at the moment we’re really looking into a storm of events that really question expertise, trust in science.

And the challenge to the trust in the scientific process and new knowledge and evidence that it generates, I think, is a serious perspective around the erosion of social cohesion.

So, in the opening session, Professor Jen Woods was talking about this sort of post-trust world and this observation that there’s a lack of trust in experts and how, where that’s taking us as a society.

And I think it’s really, this is a really fascinating area, because there’s something here about the the contract that exists between science and society, and how that has changed.

So, if we think about 80 years ago, we had an understanding that governments would fund scientists.

They had a lot of freedom and autonomy, and there was a lot of trust there that what the scientists discovered would be valuable and would bring about good in society.

And we saw lots of things emerge from that. I think washing machines is a great example, for example.

But out of that also came some things that maybe were more questionable, people weren’t quite so sure about.

And there has been a notable shift in the way that society and science interact with each other, and you could argue that where we are today is much more of a transactional relationship, where there are certain needs in society that are put to the science community.

And those are the areas where we would like science to focus, to find solutions that will benefit society and often the country within which those scientists are working.

So I think that overarching change in the way that we work within society is quite interesting

And I think it speaks a lot about the value and importance of science being done with and for people, not to and at them.

And there’s also something very interesting then about this, is this role of experts, and this idea that there’s a production in trust in experts.

And I just find this very fascinating because what we mean by trust is quite variable.

So the work from the Pew Research Institute talks about, they do lots of surveys to look at where where is trust in society, and actually scientists are actually quite high up and they haven’t fallen hugely.

So other experts have lost trust, but scientists are still quite high up.

Where the trust goes down is when scientists are starting to get involved in policymaking.

So that’s the nuance here, that there’s trust in science and there’s trust in scientific experts.

But there’s less confidence when those experts are perceived to be moving outside of their specialist domain and into more applied settings.

So I think there’s something very important here about how do we navigate a world where we believe that science has a huge amount to offer society, where science embedded into the way that we build our societies is going to add value and bring about things that we would want to uphold in society.

But how do we do that in a way where there is dialogue and transparency in terms of what can science do, what questions can it ask, what answers can it give, and not overstretch or end up putting science in a place where it probably isn’t meant to be.

#895. Burn replaces injured Guehi in England squad

Dan Burn and Marc Guehi were both part of England's 2026 World Cup squad

Newcastle's Dan Burn has been added to the England squad to play Croatia and Spain in the Nations League this week after Manchester City defender Marc Guehi pulled out with a hip injury.

Guehi was substituted at half-time of City's loss at Nottingham Forest on Saturday and manager Enzo Maresca said afterwards the centre-back had requested to come off because of the injury.

BBC Sport revealed on Sunday that the 26-year-old was having a scan to determine the severity of the ongoing issue, and the defender has now been ruled out of this week's matches.

The former Crystal Palace captain has been a mainstay of Thomas Tuchel's team since his appointment as England head coach in January 2025.

Guehi started in all but one of England's games at the World Cup and all four of the team's Nations League fixtures in September and October.

Burn has 11 international caps and was also part of Tuchel's squad for the World Cup, where he made two substitute appearances.

The 34-year-old has not featured for the Three Lions since after he missed the previous international break with an ankle injury.

England face Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, before travelling to Madrid to face World Cup winners Spain on Saturday.

#891. Kim Kardashian's SKIMS Addresses Backlash Over $148 Advent Calendar

Kim Kardashian's clothing brand SKIMS responded to social media blowback it received for its $148 advent calendar, which was deemed by a fan as a "box of pranks."

After Kim Kardashian's clothing brand faced criticism over its $148 advent calendar, the brand acknowledged it is "aware of the feedback" of its accessories advent calendar, telling TODAY.com in a Nov. 8 statement that it is now offering refunds because "for some, the calendar didn’t meet expectations."

"We have personally contacted every customer who purchased the calendar and offered them a choice of a full refund or a SKIMS credit to put towards other products,” the statement read. "We want every customer to be truly happy with what they receive from SKIMS. Their feedback matters to us and will directly shape how we approach future releases."

The limited edition product—which is currently marked as waitlisted on the SKIMS website—was marketed as "featuring twelve days of surprises," including "playful items and everyday favorites" like hair accessories and keychains.

But customers weren't happy with what the advent calendar contained, so much so that people called it a "scam" on social media while demanding their money back.

In one video that has garnered nearly 65 million views on TikTok, a "pissed off" customer unboxed the advent calendar to reveal keychains, bobby pins, ornaments, hair ties and other trinkets that left her dissatisfied.

"Kimberly, you’re genuinely about to piss me off,” the creator said in her viral video. “This is way too expensive."

Users were quick to back her up in the comments, calling the product a "box full of pranks" and saying that it feels like she was "cleaning out Kim's nightstand."

Another commenter wrote that the advent calendar featured "basically everything that falls between my car seats," while a third declared that she "just saved so many people money" by posting the contents of the product.

SKIMS is no stranger to controversy. In fact, Kardashian herself responded to backlash her brand received after it released a faux public hair thong last year.

"I'm shocked," she admitted to E! News last October. “It got so much attention—we've been laughing and talking about it all day long.”

The Kardashians star added at the time that it "was just a fun, silly idea" that came from a shoot she did.

Kardashian isn't the only celeb with a notable company. Keep reading for more celebs with beauty brands...

The one and only Rihanna changed the game when she came out with her Fenty Beauty line in 2017. Not only did she release 40 foundation shades, forging a new industry standard, but she has since created innovative and exciting products. She also released Fenty Skin and Fenty Hair.

Selena launched Rare Beauty in September 2020. The brand's initial release featured a 12-range lineup. From foundation, makeup tools and liquid lipsticks to liquid liner, blushes and more, Rare Beauty has all your bases covered.

The Grammy winner launched her new haircare line, Cécred, which features an eight-piece collection that helps cleanse, condition and repair tresses.

"My entire life and career, I've worn my hair in so many different ways: natural, flat-ironed, braids, colored, weaves, wigs," Beyoncé said in a press release shared with E! News. "I want everyone to have the freedom to express their hair in ways that make them feel good."

Mother Monster delighted her fans when she released her own cosmetics brand, Haus Laboratories, in 2019. While the songstress is no stranger to the beauty world, she decided to create something for everyone. From glimmering lipsticks to long-lasting shadows, her makeup has become a holy grail. And in June 2022, Lady Gaga "re-imagined" her brand with completely new products, a new retailer and more.

“I set out to create Henry Rose with a very clear vision," she told Elle Canada in 2024, "which was to create a fine fragrance that met three equally important criteria: disclosed 100 percent of its ingredients, met the strict health and safety standards of the Environmental Working Group, and could compete in the mainstream marketplace."

Ever wonder how the '90s super looks so dang good? The 54-year-old star credits her skincare company, Meaningful Beauty. From neck treatments to SPF-infused day creams to plumping lip gloss, there's a little bit of everything.

"This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has revealed a glimpse of its next X-plane, known as the X-70 Fractal.

Or at least what it thinks the X-70 will look like once built. The agency released a short statement on Wednesday (Nov. 4) announcing the X-plane, or experimental plane, declaring it to be a highly maneuverable test bed with a "rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology," allowing NASA to swap both external and internal components on-the-fly. This modular architecture will allow NASA to "explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight," according to the agency's statement.

The announcement was made alongside an AI-generated image showing two canted vertical tail fins emerging from swirling smoke. Little can be gleaned from the image about what final form the X-70 might take, but the tail fins are somewhat reminiscent of the Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor or Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet.

"The X-70 Fractal gives NASA a crewed, high-performance platform to test advanced flight-control, maneuverability, and other cutting-edge technologies in real flight," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in the statement. The NASA chief called the aircraft "just one part of this new beginning for aeronautics" and said that the agency expects the X-70 to make its first flight within two years.

"This is why people come to NASA: to build, to learn, and most importantly, to fly," Isaacman added.

NASA's statement fleshes out a few details about the X-70's capabilities. According to the agency, Fractal will fly at a cruise speed of Mach .75, about the same as a Boeing 737 Classic. The X-70 will be able to reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet (13.7 kilometers), and will have a range exceeding 1,726 miles (2,777 kilometers, or 1,500 nautical miles).

The X-70 Fractal will also be able to carry around 2,000 pounds (900 kg) of experimental payloads both internally and externally, which will allow for a "wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities," NASA said in the statement.

NASA adds it will have a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds (4,535 kilograms), around the same weight as the Scaled Composites- and Northrop Grumman-developed Model 437 Vanguard experimental aircraft. In fact, the two aircraft share a similar silhouette — at least in the AI image of the X-70 Fractal NASA has released so far.

The agency's most recent X-plane, the X-59, has been flying for over a year. That jet features a radical long-nosed geometry without a forward windscreen; pilots fly by way of an augmented reality screen that combines views from sensors and a forward-facing camera.

That geometry dampens the shockwaves coming off of the X-59 when it flies faster than the sound barrier, allowing it to fly at speeds over Mach 1 without the thunderous sonic booms that typically accompany supersonic flight.

There are numerous experimental aircraft being developed by private companies, such as Boom Supersonic's X-1 jet, which, like the X-59, aims to develop technologies that lessen the auditory impact of sonic booms on the ground.

In terms of other government X-plane projects, Boeing is working on the F-47, a next-generation stealth fighter for use by the U.S. military, and DARPA, the Pentagon's research agency, has an X-plane project of its own known as CRANE.

Brett is curious about emerging aerospace technologies, alternative launch concepts, military space developments and uncrewed aircraft systems. Brett's work has appeared on Scientific American, The War Zone, Popular Science, the History Channel, Science Discovery and more. Brett has degrees from Clemson University and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. In his free time, Brett enjoys skywatching throughout the dark skies of the Appalachian mountains.

#889. Kettering Town 'cannot hide' from racism problem

Kettering Town's director of football said the club could no longer hide behind "the comforting lie" that the abuse came from "a small minority"

Non-league Kettering Town have said they "can no longer hide" from the issue of racism after a visiting player was allegedly subjected to "sickening" abuse.

Redditch United player Dan Sweeney said he was targeted by a Kettering supporter during Saturday's Southern League Premier Division Central tie at the Poppies' Latimer Park stadium, which the hosts won 2-1.

The incident comes after a match official reported alleged racial abuse at a Kettering fixture last season, and a previous instance of alleged racist abuse against a Redditch player at Latimer Park in 2017.

In a statement, Kettering director of football Fabian Forde said the "poison" of racism went beyond matchdays.

He also spoke out against the presence of what he called "festering" racism on the club's fans forums.

Writing on the club's website, external, Forde said: "Let's be completely honest with ourselves: this is not the first time. We can no longer hide behind the comforting lie that 'it's just a small minority' or 'they don't reflect the majority of our fans'.

"Every single time we dismiss hate by calling it a minority issue, we minimise the damage. The truth is, if the majority stays silent, that small minority becomes our identity.

"They tarnish our reputation in the eyes of opposition players, fans, and officials. They make our club look like a haven for bigotry. Is that really who we want to be?"

Forde added that the club could not "keep sending out generic statements that mean nothing" and urged fans to support "real cultural change" by taking responsibility for calling out the perpetrators of racist abuse.

He said: "To the majority of our fans, the good, decent people who love this club for the right reasons, we are pleading with you.

"We need you to stand up. We need you to confront this minority head-on. If you see someone typing hate online, call them out. If you hear someone shouting abuse next to you on a Saturday afternoon, don't look away.

"Tell a steward. Identify them to the club. Why are we protecting people who are actively destroying the reputation of the club we love?"

Northamptonshire Police said Saturday's alleged incident had not yet been reported to officers

Northamptonshire Police said they had "not identified any report relating to this [Saturday's] allegation."

However, the force added: "It may be that any report is awaiting allocation or has been made to another police force. Should a report be made elsewhere and the alleged offence be found to have taken place within Northamptonshire, we would take ownership of the investigation.

"We note Kettering Town FC's statement that it is working with its security team, stewards and the relevant authorities to identify those responsible, and we would encourage anyone who believes they have been the victim of a crime to report it to police.

"Racial abuse has no place in football or wider society, and any reports made to us will be assessed and investigated appropriately."

In a statement, external, Redditch United chairman David Faulkner said: "I particularly welcome Kettering Town's commitment to working with its security team, stewards and the relevant authorities to identify those responsible.

"It is vital that this matter is taken seriously and that appropriate action follows.

"Tackling racism requires more than statements. It requires leadership, accountability and a collective willingness to challenge unacceptable behaviour whenever and wherever it occurs.

"We must never allow incidents like this to become normalised, dismissed or simply forgotten once the immediate attention has passed."

The Football Association has also been approached for comment.

#888. Why JWoww Is "Holding on for Dear Life" With Daughter Meilani

Jenni "JWoww" Farley reflected on navigating motherhood with her tween daughter Meilani during an exclusive E! News interview at the Netflix Steps premiere: "I have a 12-year-old turning 20."

Jenni "JWoww" Farley's life tends to get crazy and loud thanks to her kids.

The Jersey Shore alum shared what it's really like being mom to her and ex Roger Mathew's daughter Meilani, 12, and son Greyson, 10, especially as her eldest navigates adolescence.

"Oh, they're bad," JWoww playfully told E! News in an exclusive interview at the world premiere of Netflix's Steps on Nov. 8. "We're just holding on for dear life. I have a 12-year-old turning 20, and sometimes, that is not easy."

In fact, the reality star admitted that she and husband Zack Clayton turned the NYC occasion into a date night since even they "have to get away and enjoy time together."

Although parenting a tween isn't always a fairy tale, JWoww would never put a stahp to the ups and downs that come with it.

"When I was a teenage girl, I was only being raised by my father," she recalled. "So, what I always ask from my daughter and my son is to give me grace because this is also my first time being a mom."

She also emphasized that she's learning as she goes while raising a "very, very strong and independent" daughter.

"She knows who she wants to be, and I never want to dim that light," JWoww reflected. "I just want to be by her side as her friend while also trying to be her parent. It's a very fine line you have to walk when it comes to friendship versus parenting."

The 41-year-old credits her parenting style to the most important pillars of her life: gym, tan and the millennial experience.

"We all go to bed in tears, worrying about the little tiny things like, 'Did we screw up? Did we do this? Did we do that?'" she explained. "It all comes from love because we never want them to experience what we did growing up, and we want our children to have a voice in the house."

"But having that voice comes with challenges," she conceded, "because they're going to talk back and they're going to give you their opinion, and that opinion might be something you don't want."

And she is especially grateful for the peace that Zack—whom she wed in June—has brought during this time in their lives.

"Spending seven years together before getting married, there's something beautiful about that because I truly believe you know the person inside and out," she said. “When we decided to take our relationship to the next chapter, it wasn't about anything other than solidifying the fact that we will just grow old together."

As JWoww and Zach embrace life as newlyweds, keep reading for a closer look at their sweetest family moments.

"Back to where it all started," Jenni shared on Instagram back in September. "Strolled by where we had our first date @zackcarpinello."

"SISTASSSSS... oh look, another glorious morning! Makes me sick!!!! #hocuspocus," Jenni shared on Instagram when celebrating Halloween early.

The famous couple turned heads for all the right reasons when attending the 2019 MTV Video Music Awards.

As Jenni's relationship grew, the MTV reality star felt comfortable having her kids around her man.

"I thought you did amazing. She was really nervous and she did fantastic like always," Zach told his girlfriend after she presented at the 2019 CMT Music Awards.

Early on in their relationship, Jenni and Zach enjoyed a trip to Universal Studios to explore The Wizarding World of Harry Potter.

Before breaking up, Zach appeared on Jenni's MTV reality show as well as her YouTube channel.

Over Memorial Day weekend, the twosome headed to Las Vegas where they hit up a party with DJ Tiësto at the Hakkasan Night Club at MGM Grand.

During their trip out west, the couple hit up the Sugar Factory American Brasserie at Fashion Show Mall Las Vegas with a group of friends and later attended the All Elite Wrestling (AEW) Double or Nothing event.

#887. Chelsea staff warned over Fantasy Premier League use

Joao Pedro hasn't played for Chelsea since a win against Everton last month

Chelsea have warned staff to be careful about inadvertently revealing team news through Fantasy Premier League after Joao Pedro's injury appeared to have been disclosed through team selections.

An email was sent to staff reminding them of the potential consequences of using inside information when playing Fantasy Premier League or other public gaming platforms, where team selection choices could reveal which players are unavailable or close to returning.

It followed leaks before the 2-0 home defeat by Tottenham, when Pedro was a surprise absentee because of what has since emerged to be a quad injury.

Several influential Fantasy Premier League content creators claimed to have seen evidence that forward Morgan Rogers, along with several members of Chelsea staff, had removed Pedro from their Fantasy Premier League teams before kick-off at Stamford Bridge, despite no club announcement having been made about his injury.

Asked about the matter by BBC Sport after the defeat, Xabi Alonso said he was unaware of the situation. He replied: "I am not into the fantasy team thing, so I didn't know that."

Since joining Chelsea in the summer, Alonso, 44, has generally been guarded when discussing injury issues in media conferences.

Chelsea have also previously experienced problems with leaks.

During former manager Liam Rosenior's four-month spell in charge last season, team selections were leaked before both legs of the club's Champions League defeat by Paris St-Germain.

It also later emerged former defender Marc Cucurella's barber had revealed on social media that Pedro and Cole Palmer would miss a trip to Brighton last season after discussing the matter with his client.

With regard to Fantasy Premier League, no further restrictions are expected because Chelsea regard the incident as an isolated case that can be managed through greater awareness among players and staff.

There have been many further examples, claiming to suggest players from clubs like Arsenal, Liverpool, Leicester and Newcastle made revealing changes to their teams, while BBC Sport has identified accounts believed by Fantasy Premier League trackers to be linked to high-profile players and figures at clubs across the division.

The highest-profile example was arguably the revelation of then Aston Villa forward Jack Grealish's omission from the squad before a match against Leicester City in February 2021.

Then Leicester manager Brendan Rodgers later said he had been aware of rumours surrounding Grealish's injury absence before the match, which his side won.

More than 11 million people are said to play Fantasy Premier League, which has become an increasingly prominent part of the wider football ecosystem.

Although there are strict rules prohibiting gambling, the Premier League offers no specific guidance to clubs on how, or whether, those involved in the game should participate in Fantasy Premier League.

Instead, it is generally treated as a matter for individual clubs to manage themselves.

#885. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins is the 1st Black woman to command a space mission. Will we see more diversity in the future on the final frontier?

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Latest space missions, discoveries and exploration updates.

Stargazing tips, cosmic events and expert insights on the universe

Start exploring exclusive deals, expert advice and more

Space news, cosmic updates and expert insights straight to your inbox.

Breaking space news, the latest updates on rocket launches, skywatching events and more!

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Sign up to our monthly entertainment newsletter to keep up with all our coverage of the latest sci-fi and space movies, tv shows, games and books.

Discover this week's must-see night sky events, moon phases, and stunning astrophotos. Sign up for our skywatching newsletter and explore the universe with us!

Space.com's Sci-Fi Reader's Club. Read a sci-fi short story every month and join a virtual community of fellow science fiction fans!

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Jessica Watkins became commander of her mission to the International Space Station, she didn't just fulfill her duty as an astronaut — she made history.

Watkins is commanding SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which launched her and three other astronauts to the International Space Station on Oct. 1. As their Crew Dragon capsule lifted off atop a Falcon 9 rocket that day, Watkins became the first Black woman to command a crewed mission to space. Spaceflight and space science are historically white and male-dominated fields, so this milestone carries incredible significance.

"This is certainly an important milestone, I think both for our agency and for the country," Watkins said in a press briefing ahead of Crew-13's launch.

This is Watkins' second spaceflight. She previously flew on SpaceX's Crew-4 mission in 2022 and has spent more than 200 days in space to date, though that number will keep climbing for a while, as Crew-13 is set to be an approximately six-month mission. A geologist, astronaut, aquanaut and former professional rugby player, Watkins brings an incredible variety of skills to her new role as mission commander. And, in addition to what she's bringing to her colleagues on mission, she's also providing some serious inspiration for those back on Earth.

"Jessica is an inspirational symbol to a lot of people," commercial astronaut and fellow geologist Sian Proctor, who became the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft on SpaceX's private Inspiration4 mission to orbit in September 2021, told Space.com. Sian shared that the two even crossed paths years ago, when their astronaut training aligned.

"It just means so much to so many people when you see a diverse crew, and particularly women, and women of color, in leadership positions," Proctor said. "And it means something for America."

The visibility of Watkins' accomplishments and missions carries significant cultural weight. However, in addition to recognizing her many achievements, "you also should celebrate the fact that she's African American and a role model for her community," Proctor said.

Proctor, who similarly made spaceflight history with her mission, sees Watkins' role in Crew-13 as potentially more than just an exciting moment. Hopefully, she said, it will help lay the foundation for a more diverse future in human spaceflight.

"When they announced Jessica, I was super excited because it shows progress," Proctor said, sharing that she finds incredible importance in the "idea of looking at your crew and recognizing the fact that diversity makes the crew stronger."

While Watkins' historic milestone has been celebrated on social media and across the broader media landscape, NASA did not make a public statement commemorating the historic achievement. However, the agency confirmed its pioneering nature in an email to Space.com.

"NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins launched on her second spaceflight on Oct. 1, 2026, as commander of the agency's SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station, becoming the first Black woman to command a crewed space mission," a NASA spokesperson wrote in the email.

"Watkins was selected as commander of Crew-13 based on her spaceflight experience, leadership, and ability to help the mission accomplish its objectives," the spokesperson added. "As a member of NASA's astronaut corps, she represents the best of America's talent, dedication, and spirit of exploration."

To date, the U.S. and the Soviet Union are the only nations to have launched Black astronauts into space. (The Soviets beat the U.S. to this milestone, launching Cuba's Arnaldo Tamayo Méndez in 1980. NASA's Guion Bluford became the first Black American in space three years later.) But, as Proctor shared, perhaps moments like this could serve to inspire other nations to follow suit.

"We can be a leader in saying, Look, if your country is diverse and has people from all different backgrounds, you should be encouraging them to apply and have a chance to be selected," Proctor said.

And, as a commercial astronaut herself, Proctor added that commercial space can continue to play a vital role in diversifying spaceflight.

"Jared did not even hesitate when he offered me the mission pilot seat for Inspiration4," Proctor said of her own selection as mission pilot by Jared Isaacman, the tech billionaire who funded and commanded the SpaceX mission. He now serves as NASA administrator.

"Commercial space has opened up so much opportunity and access. We are celebrating that because that's another way in which the space industry has diversified so much," Proctor added. "You can look at the history of space exploration and who's had access, and then you look at what commercial's done in the last five years, and it's incredible."

On the topic of the future of space exploration, Proctor expressed confidence that future crewed moon landings with NASA's Artemis program will be diverse.

"NASA is going to send diverse crews to the moon because they've done a good job of selecting diverse individuals with different heritages in their background," she said. NASA's current astronaut corps is roughly 45% women and 25% people of color. However, to-date only 6 Black women (including Watkins) have ever flown to space.

"Do I want to see more? Do I want women of color? Absolutely. They only have two Black women," Proctor said. But with the current diversity in NASA's astronaut corps as well as the continued development of commercial spaceflight, she is optimistic about a diverse future on the moon.

So far, NASA's Artemis program has been making some inroads when it comes to diversity. With Artemis II, we saw four people launch to the moon which included Victor Glover, the first person of color to ever travel beyond low-Earth orbit, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen who became the first woman and first non-American to make the same leap.

In reaching her own historic milestone as the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft, Proctor understands that a historic moment like this carries not just incredible significance but a fair amount of personal pressure as well.

"If something goes wrong, because of who you are, maybe your gender or your ethnicity or race, you're looked at differently," she said. "When it goes right, you're not necessarily celebrated. But if it goes wrong, then that [adds to] that whole idea of 'not being qualified,'" that can come from prejudice.

"Because of who you are and the community you represent, you become the scapegoat," she added. "So, there's pressure to not have things go wrong and do everything you can to be better than the best."

But whether or not these pressures weigh on Watkins' mind, "we're all celebrating" back on Earth, Proctor said. "We're proud of her."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music

#884. Bronze named in World 11 for record ninth time

Fifpro has invited players to vote for the Women's World 11 since 2015

England defender Lucy Bronze has been named in the Fifpro Women's World 11 for a record ninth time.

Bronze is one of five England players named, with Alex Greenwood, Alessia Russo, Ella Toone and Hannah Hampton also selected.

Spain defender Irene Paredes also features for the first time since her previous selection in 2017.

Zambia striker Barbra Banda, named in the team for the third time, is the only player in the side based outside England or Spain.

The World 11 - the only global football award chosen exclusively by players - was selected through votes from 6,511 female players from 64 countries.

Goalkeeper: Hannah Hampton (Chelsea, England).

Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea, England), Alex Greenwood (Manchester City, England), Mapi Leon (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Irene Paredes (Barcelona, Spain).

Midfielders: Aitana Bonmati (Barcelona, Spain), Alexia Putellas (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Ella Toone (Manchester United, England)

Forwards: Barbra Banda (Orlando Pride, Zambia), Claudia Pina (Barcelona, Spain), Alessia Russo (Arsenal, England)

Professional players voted based on performances between 4 August 2025 and 16 August 2026, with only those with at least 20 appearances eligible.

Voters were asked to choose the three players who had performed best in each position: goalkeeper, defender, midfielder and forward.

The goalkeeper, three defenders, three midfielders and three forwards who received the most votes were selected for the World 11.

The final place was awarded to the outfield player with the next highest overall vote total, regardless of position.

#883. Injuries, noise & scalps - Wrexham's season so far

Wrexham are competing in the Championship for the second consecutive season under Phil Parkinson

With 15 games of the Championship season gone, Wrexham have steadied the ship.

Phil Parkinson's side responded to a run of three defeats in four matches by claiming four points from their home double header with promotion-hopefuls Middlesbrough and Wolverhampton Wanderers.

It ensured they entered the final international window of 2026 in positive spirits.

As the club action takes a two-week break, BBC Sport Wales looks at the highs and lows of the Red Dragons' season to date.

So how does Wrexham's performance so far this term compare to the same stage last season?

Wrexham's performances in the draws with Cardiff City and Watford early on were encouraging.

They made light work of dispatching strugglers Preston North End and have earned highly-impressive wins against top sides including Millwall, Southampton and Middlesbrough.

Defensively, Wrexham's expected goals (xG) faced of 18.17 is the fourth-best in the division.

They have also made just one error leading to a goal, the joint-best return alongside four other teams in the Championship.

Up front, Kieffer Moore - who scored 13 times for the Red Dragons in all competitions last season - has netted five goals so far this term, in addition to claiming two assists.

The Wales international's return comes from an xG figure of just 3.23, meaning he has outperformed his xG by 1.77. He has also won 68 aerial duels, with only four players in the league managing more.

Others such as Jacques Ekomie, Issa Kabore, Ben Whiteman, Joe Worrall and Callum O'Hare have shown real glimpses of settling in after joining on permanent deals in the summer.

Amid the increasing noise surrounding the club's struggles earlier on, Parkinson yet again demonstrated an impressive ability to remain grounded and get his side back on track.

In terms of the league standings, Wrexham sit six points adrift of the Championship play-off places and eight clear of the relegation zone.

So there is plenty of reason for the Wrexham faithful to remain optimistic.

A shock departure and key results - inside Wrexham's seismic week

Wrexham owners' presence uplifting - Parkinson

Parkinson 'pleased' with point against Wolves

When it comes to the numbers, only five teams have a lower xG total than Wrexham's figure of 16.80, while only three sides have managed fewer than their 50 shots on target.

Wrexham's four through balls made is - alongside Lincoln City - the joint-lowest in the division.

Home defeats by Birmingham City and West Bromwich Albion were particularly underwhelming, while the 6-0 thrashing at West Ham United represented a real low point.

Following the 2-0 loss to Blackburn Rovers in October, former Wales international Nathan Blake suggested Wrexham were losing their "fear factor" and that they were in danger of becoming "ordinary".

The Red Dragons then produced a lacklustre display as they were beaten 1-0 by Sheffield United.

It promoted a strong response from Parkinson who said he and his players would not shy away from any criticism.

After the draw with Wolves, midfielder Lewis O'Brien said of the post-Blades debrief: "I think we had to look at ourselves, deep down. It was a tough couple of days."

On the back of the 1-1 draw with Wolves, which came three days after an impressive 2-0 win over Boro, Parkinson declared his side had needed a reboot following the defeat by the Blades.

"We've had a bit of a reset this week in terms of what the performances need to look like for our supporters and everybody at the club," said the manager.

"We know we've got the capabilities to win games, but like everybody, you can easily have a capability to lose a game and you've got to be right at it.

"There's no 80% scenario in this division, everybody's got to be at it, focused and ready, and we really were ready in these two games. We can take a lot of credit from that."

Injuries certainly have not helped the club's cause, while there have been several off-the-field issues too.

The Red Dragons have been fined twice fielding ineligible players.

Chief executive officer Michael Williamson departed last week, with Shaun Harvey taking over as acting CEO.

It has clearly impacted the club's efforts in the opening third of the season.

"You always have things going on in football clubs, it's never smooth running anywhere," Parkinson said after the Wolves draw.

"But I think this has been particularly disjointed, for various reasons."

Ben Sheaf, Max Cleworth and George Thomason have all returned to action in recent weeks following significant spells on the sidelines through injury.

Nathan Broadhead is also closing in on a return, although it remains to be seen when last season's top scorer Josh Windass, Callum O'Hare and Liberato Cacace will be available.

Discussing the November international window, Parkinson said: "It's a chance to get some work in the lads who need to work and build on what we've done this week."

Unfortunately, Sam Smith is set to miss the remainder of the season and will undergo surgery this week after sustaining a serious knee injury at Sheffield United.

It will likely prompt the Red Dragons to scour the transfer market for an additional frontman in January given that Bailey Cadamarteri is the only other option behind first choice striker Moore.

Davis Keillor-Dunn could also potentially be recalled from his season-long loan spell at League One side Sheffield Wednesday - where he has scored five times in 11 appearances.

But the outlook on the campaign overall has certainly improved in the past week.

Wrexham fans hope more progress can be made over the coming months.

#881. Detroit Lions Owner Details Jack Campbell’s Neck Injury Recovery

After Jack Campbell suffered a neck injury during a Nov. 1 Detroit Lions game, the team’s owner Sheila Hamp shared insight on the linebacker’s recovery.

Jack Campbell is rooting for his team from the sidelines.

A week after the Detroit Lions linebacker was hospitalized for a neck injury, the team’s owner Sheila Ford Hamp shared how he’s keeping the team in his thoughts amid his recovery.

“I saw Jack a couple days ago,” Hamp told the team following their win against the Miami Dolphins Nov. 8 as seen in a video shared to social media, “and he was worried about all of you.”

But after the team defeated the Dolphins 19 to 9 in their latest match-up, Hamp assured, “I know he’s not now.”

“I know he’s as proud of you as I am,” Hamp told the team. “So, awesome job. Congratulations. We’re all proud of you and with you.”

Hamp’s update comes just days after Campbell—dad to son Cooper, 4 months, with wife Megan Campbell—shared his first statement since sustaining his injury Nov. 1.

“I’m incredibly encouraged by the progress I’ve made in such a short period of time,” Campbell said in a Nov. 4 message shared to the Lions’ social media accounts. “I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body.”

The 26-year-old said he felt “very optimistic” at this point, despite the “work ahead,” and noted he’s leaning on his faith to get him through this difficult time.

“My faith in God has never been stronger,” he wrote. “I know He has a plan for me and I trust that plan. I know there may be challenges ahead, but with my faith, my family, and so many people in my corner, I know we’ll get through this.”

And, of course, the NFL star—who was named captain of the Lions earlier this season—assured his teammates they still had his full support.

“I want you to know how much I love and appreciate you,” he wrote. “This team has been a family to me, and the way everyone has been there for me means everything. I’m proud to be a Detroit Lion and couldn’t ask to be surrounded by a better group of people.”

For a deeper look into Campbell’s injury and recovery journey, keep reading…

Jack Campbell was injured during the Detroit Lions’ Nov. 1 game against the Minnesota Vikings

In the fourth quarter of the teams' match-up, Campbell tackled opponent T.J. Hockenson—his third tackle of the game—and was hit on the way down.

He lay face-down on the field, unable to move after the play, and had to be carried off on a backboard by medical personnel.

Campbell was rushed to a nearby hospital to have his neck evaluated

A reporter present at the game called Campbell’s hit the “scariest moment” he’d ever witnessed at Ford Field in a Nov. 1 post on X. He also confirmed that Campbell’s wife Megan Campbell and their baby boy Cooper, who was born in July 2026, were brought down to the field to accompany the player in an ambulance.

Lions coach Dan Campbell—who has no relation to the linebacker—said the team was “thinking about him” in a post-game interview, but had no information to share.

In a post on X following the game, the Detroit Lions confirmed that Campbell was brought “to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury.”

Campbell has remained hospitalized following his injury

On Nov. 2, the Detroit Lions confirmed that Campbell was being closely monitored at the hospital.

“Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital,” the team wrote in a post on X. “Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.”

Lions coach says Campbell’s recovery update is “positive”

In a press conference one day after Campbell’s injury, Coach Campbell confirmed a heartening update on his player’s recovery.

“It’s positive,” he said. “Your prayers are working. Please continue to do that. We’ll leave it at that. Just continue to pray for him but it is positive news on Jack.”

Coach Campbell calls player an “unbelievable person”

While addressing his player’s injury, the Detroit Lions coach emphasized Campbell’s impact on the team, especially after he was tapped as team captain for this season.

“I don’t even know if I can put it into words,” Dan said during a press conference Nov. 2. “You get voted captain, that says a ton, especially with this group of guys that has been assembled. He earned every bit of that. He’s trustworthy, he’s dependable. He’d give you the shirt off his back. He’s just all heart, man. All effort."

As he put it, “There’s not a man on this team that doesn’t respect Jack Campbell and care about him,”

In an appearance on 97.1 The Ticket Radio Show Nov. 3, Coach Campbell shared an update on his player’s recovery.

“It’s not easy because he’s going to always be on our minds over here,” he said. “The good news is he is improving.”

Campbell breaks silence, says he is "very optimistic" about progress

The linebacker shared a positive update Nov. 4, noting he is "encouraged by the progress" he has made in the three days since his injury.

“I have full movement in my lower body, and I’m continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body,” he wrote in a statement shared to the Detroit Lions' Instagram. "I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic. I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”

Spacewalks are hard work, so sometimes you need to take a break for a moment and snap a gorgeous selfie with your home planet in the background.

During a pre-Halloween spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk took a moment to pose for a photograph.

In this moment, the International Space Station to which he was tethered was orbiting 267 miles (430 kilometers) above the South Atlantic Ocean down below on Earth.

During this spacewalk — the first for a Canadian since 2019 — Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon worked together to install a new roll-out solar array on the station while also performing some "get ahead" tasks to prep for the next spacewalk, which is happening today (Nov. 5).

During today's excursion, the same two astronauts will venture out into space, tethered to the space station, to install the eighth and final roll-out solar array. These eight new arrays will boost the station's available power by a total of 30%, according to NASA officials.

When we think of astronauts working in space, we might think of the important science and research they're doing aboard the station. Astronauts work on everything from biomedical research to plant science and physics experiments. But the job also includes work on the space station itself.

Sometimes they have to venture out into the vacuum of space to fix urgent problems. These situations can be tense, and there's a lot of pressure to get things absolutely right.

But even spacewalks that do relatively mundane maintenance work, like the one on Oct. 29, come with pressure. Every minute that astronauts spend outside of the space station, there are countless risk factors floating around. Earth orbit is a very harsh environment, after all, even if it does allow for some pretty amazing selfies.

#877. The super El Niño is more than a climate shock – it’s a health one, too

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Eoin McLaughlin is a professor of economics at Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, UK.

Matthias Beck is a professor of management at University College Cork, Cork, Ireland.

Food supplies will be affected by extreme weather, potentially leading to poor nutrition and disease. Credit: Joris Bolomey/AFP via Getty

The 2026–27 El Niño climate cycle is shaping up to be one of the strongest in more than a century. But the threat stretches beyond the immediate impacts of bad weather.

El Niño is part of a cycle in Earth’s climate that is linked to warmer than usual waters in the Pacific Ocean. Every few years, it brings droughts or floods to different regions. This year, sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific have already exceeded those of the four other recorded very strong El Niño events that have occurred in the past 50 years. Countries such as Panama and Indonesia are now experiencing low rainfall, and Brazil is bracing itself for wildfires. Such events have also historically had long-lived effects on economies and health. For example, the 1982–83 El Niño event resulted in a global income loss of US$4.1 trillion; for the 1997–98 one, the figure was $5.7 trillion1. And life expectancy at birth in ten (relatively wealthy) Pacific Rim countries was lowered by 0.54 years during the earlier event and by 0.37 years during the later one, relative to what would otherwise have been expected2. El Niño exposure has also been linked to childhood undernutrition, with measurable effects on height and weight3.

The latest El Niño’s effects on different places will thus depend not just on the regions’ resilience to extreme weather, but on the resilience of their food, agriculture and health systems. The World Health Organization (WHO)4 and other global organizations are aware of these risks. However, climate change, food insecurity and infectious diseases are often considered separately, despite being interdependent5.

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

The worst El Niño in recorded history is brewing — here’s how governments must prepare

We argue that the risk of catastrophe does not lie solely with the strength of this El Niño, but rather with how it interacts with other crises and local institutions. Comparatively little attention has been given to what happens when El Niño disrupts food supplies, affects what people eat and potentially changes their exposure to infectious disease.

And the latest El Niño is occurring at a time when global food systems are under pressure. Ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran have disrupted agricultural production and trade, and fertilizers are in short supply. In isolation, many countries could withstand a major El Niño, but the combined effect of several shocks could overwhelm that resilience.

These interactions might also create health risks that are less obvious. Food shortages and changes in relative prices can alter what people eat and where they obtain their food from, potentially increasing contact with animals carrying zoonotic diseases. We argue that understanding how climate, food insecurity and infectious-disease risks interact is essential to anticipating the wider health consequences of the coming El Niño.

The WHO rightly describes El Niño as ‘a risk modifier’: its health effects depend not just on the climatic shock, but also on the vulnerabilities of the populations and systems that it affects. Yet, public-health discussions have so far centred on the direct consequences of extreme weather.

The Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago in Illinois projects 451,000 extra heat-related deaths — mainly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), particularly the Sahel region of Africa — associated with this El Niño6. The World Meteorological Organization also warns of the health risks associated with extreme heat, as well as increased spread of infectious diseases linked to changes in weather patterns. A WHO assessment identifies very high risks from malnutrition; cholera due to water contamination and heat stress; and high risks from malaria, arthropod-borne viral diseases and zoonotic diseases associated with greater exposure to vectors and movement of animals in changing conditions.

These risks can be substantial. The 2022 Pakistan floods demonstrated how extreme weather can generate several public-health crises. There were considerable agricultural losses, and flooding contributed to outbreaks of malaria and waterborne diseases. This was compounded by damage to health-care infrastructure that disrupted access to essential medicines7.

Workers in the Philippines trial resilient rice varieties that can withstand droughts and floods.Credit: Ezra Acayan/Getty

But another pathway to health has garnered less attention: what happens when extreme weather disrupts food supplies?

Earlier this year, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme warned that the current El Niño could compound already high levels of food insecurity across parts of Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Caribbean8. The two agencies proposed providing anticipatory assistance to 8.8 million people. The countries they highlighted were already experiencing severe food insecurity: an estimated 57% of Somalia’s population and 51% of Haiti’s were undernourished, and 63% of South Sudan’s population was experiencing severe food insecurity.

Lower agricultural production is a concern — particularly of maize (corn) in South Africa, where output was around 40% lower than normal during the 2015–16 El Niño and about 20% lower during the 2023–24 one. More concerning is that the current El Niño is arriving alongside other shocks that will push up the cost of food9. Low-income countries have experienced the brunt of food price inflation since 2020, linked to disruptions due to COVID-19 and wars. At the height of food price inflation, 65% of low-income countries and 61% of LMICs experienced levels greater than 10%.

There is limited evidence to link previous strong El Niño events with surges in food prices. Neither 1997–98 nor 2015–16 coincided with a global food-price shock comparable to those the world has experienced since 2020 (see ‘Food price spikes’). However, global trends can conceal substantial local price increases. During the 2015–16 El Niño, for example, maize prices rose sharply in Mozambique while the global FAO Food Price Index was falling. Over the past few years, South Sudan has experienced large increases in domestic food prices, driven by conflict, currency depreciation and deteriorating economic conditions. These examples illustrate how, even when global food prices remain relatively stable, local vulnerabilities can amplify food-price shocks and trigger shortages — which can alter what people eat and where they obtain their food from, potentially increasing contact with animals carrying zoonotic diseases.

Source: UN Food and Agriculture Organization

On the basis of timing alone, it is tempting to associate strong El Niños with pandemics. Several — including the 1889–90 Russian influenza, 1918–19 Spanish flu and 1957–58 Asian flu pandemics10 — have preceded or occurred around the time of strong El Niños11. And a moderate one coincided with the 2009 swine flu pandemic. However, such coincidences tell us very little about whether the events were causally connected.

More useful historical evidence can be gleaned from cases in which there is clear evidence that link climatic shocks, food insecurity and health outcomes. Take the 1876–78 El Niño, which was one of the strongest in recorded history. The event contributed to widespread drought across Asia, Africa and the Americas. It also coincided with some of the largest famines of the nineteenth century12. However, the outcomes differed from place to place.

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

How fertilizer shortages caused by the energy crisis threaten food security

In India and China, disruption of normal monsoon seasons contributed to severe famines with millions of deaths13. What drove the disruptions was not just crop failures, but also people’s inability to purchase the food that remained. Price increases and income losses, shaped by local markets, pushed people into hunger and poverty. And the state was neither able nor willing to provide relief.

Ireland had a different experience. Heavy rainfall and one of the coldest winters in modern times14 led to poor harvests and food shortages. But there was no widespread famine, thanks in part to supplies being brought in by rail and from overseas and international aid. Instead, the crisis fed social unrest — a rebellion known as the Land War, during which tenant farmers rose up against their landlords over high rents amid falling incomes.

Thus, the same climatic disturbance can have very different outcomes depending on the economic and institutional conditions in which it occurs. The current El Niño is hitting an already-stressed food system: although international trade can offset local shortages, it can also worsen food scarcity through higher prices and export restrictions. The consequences are hard to predict, but planning can avert the worst outcomes.

Food shortages raise another issue. What do people do when their usual sources are no longer available or become too expensive? They look for alternatives, just as consumers do each day in supermarkets. This might affect their health and nutrition. And the search for alternatives could change which animals people come into contact with and what people eat.

Food insecurity can increase reliance on wild meat, creating another route through which a food shock can become a public-health problem15. Outbreaks of Ebola in Africa have been associated with contact with infected wildlife, including through hunting, butchering and preparing bushmeat.
